analysis.one_liner: Requires employers with 15 or more workers to give employees seven paid sick days during contagious-illness outbreaks.
analysis.headline: Introduced during the 2009 H1N1 flu outbreak, the bill was referred to the Senate health committee and never received a hearing, a vote, or floor action before the Congress ended in January 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required employers with 15 or more employees to provide at least seven days of paid sick time a year, usable when a worker or their child has symptoms of a contagious illness like the flu, has been exposed and told to stay home, or when a workplace, school, or child care program closes because of an outbreak. Part-time workers would get a pro-rated share. It was written as a temporary two-year measure tied to the H1N1 pandemic, and it barred employers from firing or punishing workers for using the leave. It never advanced past its referral to committee.
analysis.who_benefits: The tens of millions of workers who have no paid sick leave — the bill's findings say 50 to 60 million workers lack it, and only 1 in 4 low-wage workers has paid sick days. These are disproportionately workers in public-facing jobs like food service, retail, and child care. Workers would also gain protection against being fired for staying home sick, and parents would be able to stay home with a sick child or when school closes. Public health would benefit: the bill cites CDC findings that sick workers transmit flu to 8–12% of coworkers and that staying home could cut pandemic infections by 15–34%.

how_it_helps.text: Provides at least 7 days of paid sick time annually for full-time employees (pro-rated for part-time) at employers with 15 or more workers, usable for their own or a child's contagious illness, exposure-related quarantine, or closures of a workplace, school, or child care program.

Makes it illegal for an employer to fire, discriminate against, or retaliate against a worker for using the leave, including counting it under attendance policies, and gives workers a right to sue for remedies modeled on the Family and Medical Leave Act.

Addresses a public health gap: the bill's findings cite Bureau of Labor Statistics data that 50–60 million U.S. workers have no paid sick leave, only 1 in 4 low-wage workers has it, and CDC research showing staying home with flu could reduce pandemic infections by 15–34%.

analysis.who_pays: Covered employers — businesses with 15 or more employees — would bear the cost of paid leave they do not already provide, plus compliance costs for posting notices and avoiding retaliation. Employers with existing policies providing at least 7 equivalent days would owe nothing extra. Costs would fall hardest on labor-intensive sectors like food service, retail, and hospitality where sick leave is least common.

drawbacks.text: It imposes a direct cost on employers, including small businesses just above the 15-employee threshold, at a time when the economy was recovering from recession; the bill itself acknowledges the need to be 'feasible for employers.'

The mandate was temporary — it would terminate two years after enactment — so it addressed the immediate pandemic rather than establishing a permanent sick leave standard, limiting its lasting benefit.
Employers could face lawsuits and regulatory compliance burdens; enforcement allows employees to bring collective actions in federal or state court, with a one-year statute of limitations.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to workers and public health was substantial in scale — 50 to 60 million people without sick leave, during an active pandemic — while the cost to employers was capped by design: seven days, a 15-employee threshold, credit for existing policies, and a two-year sunset. The main honest objection is the compliance cost for small and low-margin employers, and the fact that a temporary mandate leaves the underlying gap unresolved. On balance this was a modest, time-limited mandate with broad benefit to low-wage workers.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was read twice in the Senate and referred to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which never took it up; no hearing, vote, or floor action ever happened, and it died when the 111th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Christopher Dodd introduced the bill on November 17, 2009, during the 2009 H1N1 influenza pandemic, joined by Democratic senators Harkin, Franken, Brown, and Merkley.
The Senate referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions the same day.
The committee took no further action of any kind — no markup, no vote — and the bill never reached the Senate floor, dying when the Congress ended on January 3, 2011.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers that would have had to provide new paid sick leave, particularly in retail, food service, and hospitality, were spared the cost, and workers without paid sick days gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers who would have owed paid leave

for.name: Sen. Christopher Dodd
for.role: U.S. Senator from Connecticut; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Pandemic Protection for Workers, Families, and Businesses Act in the Senate during the H1N1 outbreak.

for.name: Sens. Tom Harkin, Al Franken, Sherrod Brown, and Jeff Merkley
for.what_they_did: Joined Dodd in introducing the bill; Harkin chaired the committee it was referred to.

against.name: Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
against.role: Committee of referral; chaired by a Democrat
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, no markup, no vote — leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so no roll-call record exists; its sponsor and original co-introducers were all Democrats, and no Republicans are recorded as supporting it.

industries.industry: Employers with 15 or more employees, especially retail, food service, and hospitality
industries.note: These employers would have had to pay up to seven days of sick leave they do not currently provide; the bill's findings note that low-wage workers in frequent public-contact jobs are the least likely to have it. The cost falls on the same firms whose workers would gain the protection.
Fewer sick people coming to work means fewer infections and, per the bill's cited CDC estimates, a 15–34% reduction in pandemic spread, easing pressure on providers and public health systems.
